Lesson · 25 min

Organize with Labels, Filters, Search, and Snooze

Use labels instead of folders, find any message in seconds with search operators, let filters sort mail as it arrives, and snooze messages until you need them.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • ✓Create a label, apply it to a conversation, and explain how labels differ from folders
  • ✓Find messages with search operators such as from:, subject:, has:attachment, and older_than:
  • ✓Create a filter from your search and apply it to mail you already have
  • ✓Snooze a message so it returns to your inbox when you need it

Lesson Notes

Read through the key concepts before you try the challenge.

Labels instead of folders

On the job

You keep the Parkview office mailbox organized.

Vendor invoices from Russo Plumbing and Bright Clean Services are scattered through the inbox. Denise wants all vendor mail in one place, out of the inbox, without losing anything, and Grace Holloway's question about the roof estimate shouldn't clutter your inbox until the estimate is ready.

Your task: Set up Gmail so vendor mail sorts itself and nothing slips through the cracks.

Gmail organizes mail with labels. A label works like a tag: one conversation can have several labels, such as Vendors and Elm Street Apartments, and still be in the inbox. A folder can only hold a message in one place. Labels are private: only you see the labels you put on your mail, and the people you write to don't.

  1. To create a label, on the left next to Labels, select Create new label (+). Enter a name and select Create. To put it inside another label, check Nest label under and pick the parent.
  2. To label a conversation, check the box next to it (or open it), select Labels (the tag icon) at the top, check the label, and select Apply.
  3. To move a conversation to a label, select Move to instead. Move to adds the label and takes the conversation out of the inbox.
  4. To see everything with a label, select the label on the left.
If you're used to Outlook, a Gmail label is like a folder you can use more than once, and a Gmail filter is like an Outlook rule.

Search like a pro

Type in Search mail at the top and press Enter. Plain words search everything. Search operators narrow it down. You can combine them: from:russo has:attachment finds only Russo Plumbing messages with attachments.

Filters sort mail as it arrives

A filter is a rule Gmail runs on new mail. It checks each message against your search and then does what you chose: skip the inbox (archive it), mark it as read, star it, apply a label, forward it, delete it, never send it to Spam, always or never mark it as important, or put it in a category.

  1. In the search box, select Show search options (the sliders icon).
  2. Fill in what to look for, such as From: tony@russoplumbing.example. Select Search first if you want to preview the matches.
  3. Select Create filter.
  4. Check what the filter should do, for example Skip the Inbox (Archive it) and Apply the label: Vendors.
  5. To sort the mail you already have too, check Also apply filter to matching conversations.
  6. Select Create filter.

You can also start a filter from a message: check the box next to it, select More (three dots), and choose Filter messages like these. To change or remove a filter later, go to Settings › See all settings › Filters and Blocked Addresses, and select edit or delete next to it.

Be careful with Delete it and Skip the Inbox. A filter that's too broad (for example, everything with the word “invoice”) can hide messages you needed. Test the search first and look at what it finds.

Snooze

Snooze takes a message out of your inbox until a time you choose, then brings it back to the top of the inbox. Point to the message and select Snooze (the clock) on the right, or open it and select Snooze at the top. Choose a time such as Later today or Tomorrow, or pick a date and time. Snoozed messages wait under Snoozed in the main menu, and you can search for in:snoozed.

Worked example

Organizing vendor mail

Keep vendor mail together and out of the inbox.

  1. 1

    Create a Vendors label.

    One place to see every vendor message, whichever building it's about.

  2. 2

    Search from:russo has:attachment.

    Checks exactly which messages a Russo Plumbing filter would catch, before anything moves.

  3. 3

    Create a filter: From tony@russoplumbing.example, Skip the Inbox, Apply the label Vendors, and apply it to matching conversations.

    Old and new invoices land under Vendors automatically, so the inbox stays a to-do list.

  4. 4

    Snooze Grace's roof estimate question until tomorrow.

    You can't answer until the estimate arrives. Snooze brings it back when you can.

Result: Vendor mail sorts itself, and the inbox shows only what needs you today.

🔑 Search first, then turn a good search into a filter.

Challenge

Apply what you've learned in this lesson.

Organize part of your own Gmail.

  1. Create a label named BEOC.
  2. Search for messages from one sender who writes to you often, using from: and the sender's name or address. Write down the search you used.
  3. Turn that search into a filter that applies the BEOC label (don't choose Delete it). Check Also apply filter to matching conversations.
  4. Open the BEOC label and take a screenshot.
  5. Snooze one message until tomorrow, and open Snoozed to see it.
Deliverable: Submit your search, a screenshot of the BEOC label, and a screenshot of Snoozed to your instructor or course folder. If you can't use Gmail, complete the practice simulation and submit its results page.
